<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Age-friendly cities and communities (AFCC), together with initiatives to combat ageism, are recognised as two of the four action areas of the United Nations (UN) Decade of Healthy Ageing, have received global attention. However, there is a lack of understanding regarding the distinct experiences of older adults in their cities and communities, as well as the extent to which these experiences are linked to their perceptions of ageism. Using a sample of 398 older adults from four cities in Colombia, a latent profile analysis was conducted via the manual three-step method, incorporating demographic covariates and distal outcomes, to identify distinct AFCC profiles among older adults. Three AFCC profiles emerged from the analysis: “high AFCC except financial support” (59.5%), “mixed AFCC with low outdoor spaces/buildings and financial support” (31.4%), and “low AFCC except respect/inclusion” (9.1%). Older adults with disabilities had a higher probability of belonging to the “mixed AFCC with low outdoor spaces/buildings and financial support” group, while age, gender, and subjective social status showed no significant association with profile membership. In addition, ageism experiences differed among the three profiles, as older adults with lower AFCC scores reported higher levels of ageism. The results suggested both a potential method effect associated with negative items in the AFCC, as well as differences in the contexts captured by the AFCC and ageism measures, with the former anchored in community environments and the latter spanning broader interpersonal, institutional, and self-directed experiences. In sum, our findings highlight the need to understand the distinct patterns in how older adults perceive their cities and communities, as well as identify those who may be “at risk” in specific domains.</jats:p>
title: Latent profiles of the perceived age-friendliness of cities and communities in Colombia: relations to ageism experiences in later life

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Research has shown that adults prefer to remain in their own homes as they age. Care homes are expensive and as the population ages, availability is likely to become more limited and unaffordable to many. Live-in care, when a paid worker moves into the care recipient’s home to provide support, offers a potential alternative to residential care. This is the first scoping review of research on live-in care with a particular focus on people living with dementia. It seeks to reframe understanding of long-term care options for people with dementia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review followed conduct guidelines as described by the JBI. Systematic searches were conducted using seventeen bibliographic databases and sources rich in grey literature for quantitative or qualitative studies investigating live-in care. Results were double screened by two independent reviewers. Data were extracted and checked. Common findings found during data extraction were translated into themes. A lay advisory group was also consulted as to which themes were most relevant to them.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Most studies were qualitative in nature with a focus on the experience of the live-in care worker. In all studies live-in care workers were from countries outside of where they worked. Common themes arising from the findings of the studies included: motivations for choosing live-in care; relationships between live-in carer and care recipient and their families; exploitation of care workers and perceived quality of the care provided. Only seven studies focused on live-in care for people with dementia. These results address a critical gap in knowledge about a global form of care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Live-in care offers a promising alternative to residential care. Existing studies highlight a range of issues that should be addressed with live-in care arrangements, including exploitation of the workforce, cultural differences between workers and the families, a lack of training for live-in care workers and the importance of good relationships with this model of care. This scoping review identifies a previously unrecognised pattern, namely a focus on the live-in care worker, rather than the experiences of those receiving care. More studies investigating live-in care specifically for people living with dementia would help inform whether this model of care is effective for them.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The adverse effects of potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) use in older adults are one of major public health burdens. This study aimed to examine the association between PIM use and healthcare utilizations and costs among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used the Korean National Health Insurance Service-Elderly Cohort Database in 2015–2018 with matched cohort design. A propensity score derived from 16 variables, including age, sex, index year, Charlson Comorbidity Index scores, income decile, residential status, nine main comorbidities and number of comedication, was used for 1:1 matching. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to compare the risk of hospitalization and emergency department (ED) visits 1 year after the index date between PIM users and non-users. In addition, hospitalization- and ED visit related costs were evaluated using a two part model consisting of logistic regression and generalized linear model with logit link.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 3,896 older adults aged ≥ 65 years at index date were included, comprising 1,948 PIM users and 1,948 matched non-users. All the matching variables were well balanced with absolute Standardized Mean Difference (aSMD) < 0.1. Females were 52.77% in non-users and 54.65% in users. The mean age was 73.26 (sd: 5.97) in non-users and 73.14 (sd: 5.98) in users. The results indicated that PIM users were associated with higher risk of hospitalization than non-users (adjusted HR [aHR]: 2.18, 95% CI: 1.81–2.63) and were more likely to visit the ED (aHR: 3.08, 95% CI: 2.01–4.72). Furthermore, the total healthcare costs for PIM users were 40% higher among PIM users than non-users (adjusted Cost Ratio [aCR]: 1.4, 95% CI: 1.35–1.54). Among PIM users, increasing numbers of PIMs were associated with higher total healthcare costs, as well as higher hospitalization- and outpatient-related costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PIM use was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization and ED visits, as well as higher healthcare costs. These findings highlight the importance of regular medication review and optimization of prescribing in older adults. However, PIM use should be considered within the broader context of multimorbidity and frailty, rather than as an isolated risk factor, when developing strategies to improve health outcomes in this population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Healthcare and cost burdens associated with potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults: a matched cohort study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with stroke frequently have coexisting hypertension and diabetes, a high-risk cardiometabolic profile that complicates prevention, long-term management, and health service planning. However, population-based evidence on the long-term incidence trajectory of stroke occurring with both conditions remains limited, particularly in rapidly urbanizing settings undergoing population ageing. This study examined long-term trends, age-period-cohort patterns, and future projections of incident stroke with comorbid hypertension and diabetes among older adults in Shenzhen, China.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This population-based retrospective surveillance study used data from the Shenzhen Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease Registry System. Incident stroke events registered between 1 January 2004 and 31 December 2023 among adults aged ≥ 60 years were identified, and 40,128 events with comorbid hypertension and diabetes were included. Crude incidence rates (CIRs) and age-standardized incidence rates (ASIRs) were calculated. Joinpoint regression, age-period-cohort analysis, and Bayesian age-period-cohort modeling were used to assess temporal trends, estimate age, period, and cohort effects, and project incidence trends from 2024 to 2033.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>From 2004 to 2023, the number of incident stroke events with comorbid hypertension and diabetes increased from 314 to 3,336, and the ASIR rose from 141.12 per 100,000 in 2004 to 414.78 per 100,000 in 2023. Joinpoint regression showed overall increasing trends in CIR and ASIR across the study period, with average annual percent changes of 5.44% and 6.14%, respectively, while identifying a late-period decline after 2017. Incidence levels were generally higher in males than in females. Age-period-cohort analysis showed marked age effects, elevated period-related risks in recent periods, and increasing cohort effects across successive birth cohorts. Bayesian projections suggested that both CIR and ASIR may increase from 2024 to 2033, with larger projected increases in males.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among older adults in Shenzhen, the burden of stroke with comorbid hypertension and diabetes showed a long-term upward trajectory over the study period.</jats:p>
                    <jats:p>Model-based projections suggested that the burden may increase from 2024 to 2033, particularly among males and older age groups. These findings provide population-level descriptive and projection evidence that may inform risk stratification and health service planning for ageing urban populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Long-term trends, age-period-cohort patterns, and future projections of incident stroke with comorbid hypertension and diabetes among older adults in Shenzhen, China: a population-based surveillance study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Frailty is a clinical syndrome associated with greater risk of functional limitations and dependency. However, older people with or at risk of frailty who live at home can still lead fulfilling lives, engage with their community, and maintain a good quality of life, that is,
                      <jats:italic>age in place</jats:italic>
                      well. To support this and prevent resource-intensive care use, this expert consultation survey aimed to identify proxy indicators that capture ageing-in-place experiences in community-dwelling older people with frailty.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Using a modified Delphi approach, two survey rounds were conducted to build consensus on proxy ageing-in-place indicators in relation to frailty. Eighty-nine indicators were extracted from a rapid literature review and grouped into five themes:
                      <jats:italic>Personal Characteristics of Older People</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>Place</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>Social Networks</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>Support</jats:italic>
                      , and
                      <jats:italic>Technology</jats:italic>
                      . Eighteen experts in geriatric care and gerontology rated indicators for importance for ageing-in-place and feasibility of routine measurement. Consensus for importance and feasibility was defined as mean scores ≥ 4.0 (scale 1–5), suggesting indicators were extremely/very important for ageing-in-place
                      <jats:italic>and</jats:italic>
                      extremely/very feasible to measure routinely. Public contributors, who were experts by lived experiences of frailty and ageing-in-place, also reviewed the indicators and survey findings.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Only four proxy indicators reached consensus for importance
                      <jats:italic>and</jats:italic>
                      feasibility: “physical performance and mobility”, “multimorbidity”, “sensory function”, and “pressure ulcers” (all
                      <jats:italic>Personal Characteristics</jats:italic>
                      ). Twenty-seven indicators were extremely/very important for ageing-in-place but not as feasible to measure routinely (17 related to
                      <jats:italic>Personal Characteristics</jats:italic>
                      , 4 to
                      <jats:italic>Social Networks</jats:italic>
                      , and 3 to
                      <jats:italic>Place</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic>Support</jats:italic>
                      ). Only five indicators (the four consensus indicators and “polypharmacy”) were extremely/very feasible to measure routinely. No technology-related indicators were extremely/very important or feasible to measure routinely. Mean scores of few indicators differed by experts’ occupations and areas of expertise. Public contributors generally agreed with the survey results but highlighted the importance of technology-related indicators (particularly “digital literacy”) and more integrated care records to support targeted care.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study lays the foundation for developing standardised proxy ageing-in-place indicators to monitor how older people with or at risk of frailty are living in their homes and communities. Future directions include assessing feasibility of capturing non-clinical indicators routinely; applying these indicators to guide personalised targeted interventions; and leveraging technology-related indicators to improve digital inclusion and literacy in older people to support ageing-in-place.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Proxy indicators to support independent ageing-in-place in older people with frailty: a Delphi-style expert consultation survey

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diabetes is a major global public health concern, and China bears a growing diabetes burden that calls for targeted prevention. High-income country studies link residential proximity to roadways with diabetes, yet evidence from developing countries is limited. This population-based analysis delivers robust evidence for environmental health interventions and age-friendly urban planning for Chinese older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used nationally representative data from the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). After excluding those with missing values for key variables, 4,702 adults aged ≥ 65 years entered the complete-case primary analysis. Roadway proximity and diabetes status were self-reported. Logistic regression models calculated ORs and 95% CIs with sequential adjustment for demographic, lifestyle and health covariates. Stratified analyses and interaction tests assessed effect modification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The sample included 4,702 participants (mean age 78.7 years; 55.1% men) with 13.9% diabetes prevalence. Fully adjusted ORs were 1.36 (95% CI:1.11–1.67) for residents < 100 m from major roadways and 1.31 (95% CI:1.03–1.66) for those 100–300 m away (reference group: > 300 m). A statistically significant overall trend test was obtained, yet the exposure–response relationship across distance strata was non-monotonic (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      for trend < 0.05). A borderline interaction existed between roadway proximity and smoking (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      for interaction = 0.044). Stratification showed a positive association among non-smokers (OR = 1.29, 95% CI:1.06–1.56) but no significant link in smokers (OR = 0.82, 95% CI:0.48–1.42). Given the marginal
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      -value and small smoking subgroup sample (wide CIs), this interaction needs cautious interpretation and verification in larger cohorts.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study found a significant association between proximity to major roadways and prevalent diabetes in Chinese older adults. Roadway proximity acts as a composite surrogate marker of traffic hazards, neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation and built environments, rather than merely traffic pollution or noise. These findings guide future environmental and health equity research on seniors. Longitudinal studies with objective exposure measurements are required to confirm our results and inform age-friendly urban design and geriatric health policies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Residential proximity to major roadways and prevalent diabetes in older adults: a cross-sectional study based on CLHLS

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Gendered ageism has been highlighted as an important global challenge, and progress in understanding and addressing it requires measures of ageism that are reliable, valid, and comparable across genders. However, there has been little examination of the extent to which existing measurement tools for ageism are appropriate for use within and for comparing ageism across genders. We used data collected across four diverse country contexts, Moldova, Colombia, Libya, and China (
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 1675), to examine the properties of the WHO Ageism Experiences Scale with respect to its capability for comparing ageism across genders and for illuminating selected aspects of gendered ageism — specifically, whether the scale functions equivalently across gender groups and whether men and women differ in their levels of ageism experiences and in the associations between ageism and health. Findings supported the gender measurement invariance of the scale across the reflective indicators. Results also indicated no significant differences in the levels of ageism experienced by women versus men in these contexts. However, the associations between ageism and health-related outcomes were significantly stronger for men than for women. The results supported the use of the WHO Ageism Experiences Scale across genders and highlighted a complex relationship between gender and ageism. These findings suggested that while experiences of ageism may not differ significantly between men and women, the consequences of ageism for health outcomes may vary, underlining the need for further research to better understand gendered dynamics in ageism.
                  </jats:p>
title: Illuminating gendered ageism with the WHO ageism experiences scale: a psychometric analysis and gender comparisons in a multi-country dataset

<jats:p>Introduction: The recommended target durations for moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) to promote health have been established; however, evidence supporting the use of step counts as a measure of physical activity remains limited. We aimed to compare the predictive ability of MVPA and step counts for incident disability among community-dwelling older adults.
Methods: This prospective cohort study included a total of 8664 community-dwelling older adults from a community-based setting. MVPA and step counts were measured using an accelerometer. Disability incidence and mortality rates were prospectively assessed over 60 months. Inverse probability weighting-adjusted receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was used to evaluate the predictive ability of MVPA and step counts for disability incidence, while adjusting for covariates.
Results: A total of 1,373 (15.8%) patients developed an incidental disability within 60 months. In the inverse probability weighting analysis based on the covariate model, the areas under the curve for MVPA and step counts were 0.572 (95% CI, 0.542–0.603) and 0.565 (95% CI, 0.537–0.596), respectively.
Conclusion: Among community-dwelling older adults,  step counts and MVPA showed comparable associations and predictive performance for incident disability after adjustment for background risk factors. Our findings support the use of step counts as a measure of physical activity in this population.</jats:p>
title: Time- vs. Step-Based Physical Activity Metrics for Disability Incidence in Older Adults
